name: bfs
workload: Whole-tree traversal of a home directory (about 7.6 million files) with io_uring-based async I/O queues.
claimed_speedup: bfs 3.0 about 3x faster than GNU find and 2.2x faster than the previous bfs series; fd slowest (blog snippet only); older post: 15-25% faster than GNU find 4.6.0, warm cache, 1,937,127 files
tradeoffs: find-compatible CLI, not a library; Linux io_uring path needs a recent kernel, falls back to threads/readdir.
caveats: Numbers come only from the author's blog (tavianator.com, EGRESS_BLOCKED here), seen via WebSearch snippet; repo page has no benchmark section. First-party. Hardware and flags not confirmed.
found_via: Blogs: WebSearch 'bfs breadth-first find tavianator benchmark faster than GNU find fd io_uring' (bfs 3.0: the fastest find yet!)

hardware: 64GB RAM, Samsung NVMe SSD (CPU not stated)
name: wcp
workload: Copy 20x512MiB, 7000x1MiB and 200000x1KiB files using io_uring, on a Samsung NVMe SSD with 64GB RAM.
claimed_speedup: 20x512MiB: 3.97s vs cp 8.44s vs rsync 17.26s; 7000x1MiB: 2.64s vs 8.29s vs 13.22s; 200000x1KiB: 3.92s vs 9.23s vs 8.09s
tradeoffs: Linux only, kernel 5.6+ (tested 5.8+); experimental; no portability.
caveats: README says probably not robust enough for daily use; first-party numbers; no compiler flags or cp version; stale since 2021.
found_via: Blogs: WebSearch 'fast parallel file copy tool benchmark faster than cp rsync io_uring github'

name: ripgrep
baseline: GNU grep, ag, git grep (mmap vs buffered read strategy)
workload: Recursive search of the Linux kernel tree and single-file subtitle search; mmap versus intermediate-buffer reads chosen per workload.
claimed_speedup: Blog snippet: linux_literal 0.334s without mmap vs 1.611s with mmap; subtitles_literal 0.268s with mmap vs 0.336s without. README: Linux tree search 0.082s vs git grep 0.273s
tradeoffs: Rust CLI, not callable from C++ as a library; the I/O insight (mmap slower across many files) is the reusable part.
caveats: Search engine speed dominates, not file I/O alone. mmap numbers are from the blog (burntsushi.net, not opened) via snippet only; README figure from the opened repo page. First-party.
found_via: Blogs: WebSearch 'ripgrep mmap vs read benchmark BurntSushi blog'

name: libuv io_uring file backend
workload: Async read, write, fsync, fdatasync, stat via io_uring instead of the threadpool (libuv 1.45+).
claimed_speedup: Commit message: 'an 8x increase in throughput has been observed'
tradeoffs: Linux only, kernel dependent, falls back to threadpool; some ops (access) have no io_uring path.
caveats: No workload, hardware or method given; per WebSearch commentary the 8x came from a microbenchmark that mostly stresses threadpool context switches. Baseline is libuv itself, not POSIX.
found_via: Blogs: WebSearch 'libuv io_uring file I/O threadpool speedup benchmark' (Phoronix: libuv adds io_uring support)

name: diskus
workload: Total size of a 15GB tree with 100k directories and 400k files, cold and warm disk cache.
tradeoffs: Parallel directory walk; Rust CLI, not a C++ library.
caveats: First-party README table; hardware (8-core laptop per snippet) and du version not confirmed on page.
found_via: Blogs: WebSearch 'fast disk usage scanner benchmark faster than du ncdu github getdents parallel'

name: gdu
workload: Scan of a 90GB directory with 100k directories and 400k files on a 500GB SSD, cold and warm cache.
claimed_speedup: Cold: 4.716s vs diskus 4.489s; warm: 466.1ms vs diskus 270.8ms. Snippet: 80G scanned in 6.5s vs ncdu 54s (blog, not opened)
tradeoffs: Go binary, SSD-oriented parallel scan; slower than diskus in its own table.
caveats: README table only compares to diskus (gdu is slower); the ncdu comparison is from a snippet. First-party.
found_via: Blogs: WebSearch 'fast disk usage scanner benchmark ...' (Linux Uprising gdu post)

name: couring
workload: Process 512 OBJ files with trivial, multithreaded, io_uring, coroutine and coroutine+thread-pool implementations.
claimed_speedup: Trivial 0.419s; multi-threading 0.177s; io_uring 0.368s; coroutines 0.339s; coroutines with thread pool 0.230s
tradeoffs: C++20 coroutines over liburing, Linux 5.1+; demo-quality.
caveats: Plain multithreading beats every io_uring variant; no hardware or compiler flags; speedup over trivial is modest. Reference value only.
found_via: Blogs: WebSearch 'C++ io_uring wrapper library coroutine file read benchmark faster than ifstream pread github'
